title: Major incident: planning and training
stem: ED office. Ambulance control rings: a train collision with about 40 casualties, 15 minutes away. You are the ED consultant in charge. Take the call, start the ED response, and afterwards explain to the nurse manager how the department should plan and train for such events.
notes:
Checked against the UK NHS Emergency Preparedness, Resilience and Response framework (EPRR 2022), Major Incident Medical Management and Support (MIMMS, 3rd ed.), JESIP principles (METHANE), and WHO hospital emergency response checklist (2011).

METHANE: Major incident declared/standby; Exact location; Type of incident; Hazards; Access; Number and severity of casualties; Emergency services present and required. CSCATTT: Command and control, Safety, Communication, Assessment, Triage, Treatment, Transport. ED response: activate the hospital major incident plan (cascade call-out), ED commander (consultant) and nurse coordinator with action cards, clear the ED (discharge/admit current patients), senior triage officer at the entrance, pre-assigned teams for red bays, major incident packs and numbering/ID system, blood bank/lab/radiology/theatres/ICU alerted, relatives' reception area, media liaison via hospital command, staff welfare and rotation, stand-down and debrief. Planning and training: hazard/risk assessment, written plan with action cards, surge capacity (beds, staff, supplies), communication (backup radios), exercises — tabletop, live/full-scale, and communication tests, then debrief and updating the plan (lessons identified → learned).

Your notes list 'planning and training' as a topic only. The Hong Kong HA uses its own Major Incident Control Centre and colour-coded response levels; check your cluster's current contingency plan for the exact names.
